name: Ugandan Matoke
description: Matoke, steamed and mashed green cooking bananas, is widely considered Uganda's national dish - real matoke bananas are a specific East African highland variety, and green plantain is a much closer match than sweet yellow bananas, though still not identical. Real technique wraps the peeled bananas tightly in banana leaves before steaming for close to an hour, which is what gives real matoke its pale, gently golden color and soft, cohesive mash; foil is the honest substitute for the leaves.

ingredients_full.note: peeled and left whole or halved

ingredients.note: peeled and left whole or halved

steps_detailed: Rub a little oil on your hands before peeling, since real matoke banana sap stains skin - the same is true of green plantain.
Wrap the peeled plantain tightly in a double layer of foil (standing in for banana leaves) with the salt.
Steam over simmering water 45-50 minutes, until completely soft all the way through.
Unwrap and mash thoroughly until smooth and cohesive, with no lumps.

name: Ugandan Luwombo
description: Luwombo, meat steamed inside a wrapped banana leaf parcel, is a genuine Buganda specialty traditionally reserved for special occasions and weddings - real technique steams the wrapped parcel for a long stretch, up to an hour or more, since the extended steam (not a quick finish) is what lets the banana leaf genuinely infuse the dish, sealing in an aroma open cooking cannot replicate.
steps_detailed: Brown the chicken with the onion and garlic, 8-9 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter with the tomatoes and a little water, add to the pot, and simmer 10 minutes.

Wrap tightly in foil (standing in for banana leaf) and steam over simmering water 50-60 minutes - this real, extended steam is what lets the leaf-like wrapping infuse the dish, not a quick finishing step.

name: Ugandan Groundnut Stew
description: A rich stew built on real ground peanuts, a beloved Ugandan dish shared in spirit with groundnut stews found across the wider region, real versions whisked slowly so the sauce stays smooth rather than clumping.
steps_detailed: Brown the chicken with the onion, 6-7 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter slowly with the tomatoes and a little water to keep it smooth, add to the pot.
Simmer 20-22 minutes until the chicken is tender.

name: Ugandan Rolex
description: Rolex, a rolled chapati wrapped around an omelet, is one of Uganda's most beloved street foods, its name a playful shortening of 'rolled eggs'. The real, defining technique places the raw chapati dough directly onto the omelet while the egg is still wet and cooking in the pan, which makes the two genuinely stick together - the whole thing is then flipped once as a single piece to finish, not cooked separately and rolled together afterward.
steps_detailed: Make a simple chapati dough from the flour, a little oil, and water, and let rest 15 minutes.
Whisk the eggs with the tomatoes, cabbage, and onion.
Heat the oil in a pan and pour in the egg mixture, swirling thin like a large omelet.
While the egg is still visibly wet on top, roll out a thin chapati and lay it directly on top of the cooking egg - this real technique is what makes the chapati genuinely stick to the omelet.
Flip the whole stuck-together piece as one, chapati-side down, and cook 2-3 minutes more until the chapati browns.
Roll up tightly while still warm and serve immediately.

name: Ugandan Posho
description: Posho, a stiff maize porridge, is Uganda's most essential staple starch, closely related to Kenyan ugali and eaten daily alongside stews.
steps_detailed: Whisk about a third of the cornmeal with the salt into 1.25 cups boiling water.
Gradually beat in the remaining cornmeal, stirring constantly, over medium-low heat 12-15 minutes, until very thick and smooth.

name: Ugandan Chapati
description: Chapati, a soft, layered flatbread, reflects genuine Indian culinary influence and is one of Uganda's most beloved breads, real technique coiling the rolled dough before flattening again to build real flaky layers.
steps_detailed: Work the flour with warm water and half the oil into a soft dough. Rest 20 minutes.
Roll thin, brush with the remaining oil, and coil before flattening again to build real layers.
Cook in a hot, dry pan, 2-3 minutes per side, until golden.

name: Ugandan Katogo
description: Katogo, matoke or cassava cooked together with beans or meat into one pot, is a beloved Ugandan breakfast and everyday staple, real technique mashing the plantain roughly into the beans rather than keeping them fully separate.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Cowpeas (blackeyes), immature seeds, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt

ingredients.ingredient: Cowpeas (blackeyes), immature seeds, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt

steps_detailed: Cook the onion 3-4 minutes.
Add the plantain and tomatoes with enough water to cover, and simmer 25-28 minutes.
Add the cowpeas and mash roughly together, leaving some texture rather than pureeing smooth.

Add the kale and simmer 10-12 minutes until tender.

Fry, turning, 3-4 minutes, until deeply golden.

Grill, turning, 12-15 minutes, until well charred and cooked through.

Rest 15 minutes, then roll out and cut into triangles.
Fry, turning, 3-4 minutes per batch, until deeply golden.

description: A simple tomato-based fish stew, common Ugandan home cooking near Lake Victoria, real technique cooking the onion down well first to build a proper sweet base before the tomatoes go in.
steps_detailed: Cook the onion and garlic 4-5 minutes until well softened.
Add the tomatoes and simmer 8-10 minutes.
Add the fish and simmer 8-10 minutes until just cooked through.
